catalog_quote: Tone in Buwal functions at the level of the syllable. ... Buwal has three underlying level tones, low (L), mid (M) and high (H). All three levels are found on nouns, adjectives and adverbs. Verbs, on the other hand, may only carry either low or mid tone. ... In some Chadic languages metrical structure interacts with the tonal system in terms of tone placement. The metrical structure involved is not stress (as normally understood in terms of higher pitch or intensity) but has to do with syllable weight. ... However in Buwal, it seems there is no interaction between metrical structure and tone corresponding to that found in Kera. ... This is evidence that tone is a feature of the syllable in Buwal not the foot. Furthermore, the fact that pairs such as /HLL/ and /HHL/, /LMM/ and /LLM/ were found indicates that tone is a feature of the syllable rather than the phonological word at least for noun roots. ... At this stage no interaction of metrical structure with the tonal system has been identified in Buwal. However, this would be an interesting area for futher investigation.
world_status: statement found in an open source

new_statements.rule_in_words: Buwal is described as a three-level tone language (L, M, H; verbs only L or M) in which tone is a property of the syllable, with lexical and grammatical tone contrasts. The grammar states no word-stress rule at all: the only mention of 'stress' is a definitional aside distinguishing Kera-type weight-based metrical structure from stress, followed by the finding that Buwal shows no metrical (foot/weight) effects on tone. Nothing is said about which syllable of a word is prominent.
new_statements.exceptions: None stated. Ideophones and interjections may show pitch levels beyond the three tones and 'wild changes in pitch' (§2.5, p. 68). Depressor consonants lower the tone of epenthetic vowels and of mid-tone verbal prefixes (p. 87).
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level: tone melodies given per root syllable structure for noun and verb roots, elicited in carrier frames (ārā ___ kʷāw 'it's not a ___'; sákā ___ jám 'I am ___ing also'). Phrase level: utterance-final low boundary tone (falling) and continuation high tone on the last syllable before a pause (§2.7.2.1, pp. 96-102). No explicit sentence of the form 'Buwal has no stress' — the reading is inferred from a full phonology chapter that treats tone only and reports no metrical structure.
new_statements.identity_note: Viljoen 2013 describes the Buwal of Gadala canton, Mayo-Tsanaga division, Far North Region, Cameroon (= buwa1243 / bhs; alt. names Bual, Gadala, Ma Buwal). No dialects are distinguished. The closely related Gavar (Gawar) is treated as a separate language (82-90% lexicostatistical similarity, 'significant differences in the phonological systems', thesis pp. 3-4) and is not covered by this statement. Glottolog record 687889 ('Viljoen 1983, La Trobe thesis') is a duplicate of the 2013 thesis with a wrong year.

The word 'stress' occurs once in the whole thesis (p. 87), only to say that the Kera-type metrical structure is 'not stress (as normally understood in terms of higher pitch or intensity)'; for Buwal the author finds no interaction of metrical structure with tone (pp. 88, 94).
